lines.speaker: A

points.point: Because of the struggle for life, any slight variation that is useful to an individual tends to preserve it and is generally inherited, and since only a small number of those born survive, the offspring have a better chance too.

Darwin names this principle Natural Selection, by analogy with human selection, and claims it is incessantly ready for action and immeasurably superior to man's feeble efforts, as the works of Nature are to those of Art.

Darwin uses 'struggle for existence' in a large and metaphorical sense, including dependence of one being on another and, more importantly, success in leaving progeny, not only the life of the individual.

A struggle for existence follows inevitably because all organic beings tend to increase at a high rate, so more individuals are produced than can survive and each must struggle with its own species, other species, or the physical conditions of life.
Darwin describes this as the doctrine of Malthus applied to the whole animal and vegetable kingdoms, where there can be no artificial increase of food and no prudential restraint from marriage.

Because almost all plants and animals reproduce yearly, all tend to increase geometrically and would fill every available station, so this tendency must be checked by destruction at some period of life.

Every organic being strives to increase and lives by a struggle with heavy destruction falling on young or old, so lightening any check would make numbers rise almost instantly; nature is likened to ten thousand wedges driven together by blows.
Climate, especially periodic extreme cold or drought, is the most effective check; the winter of 1854-55 destroyed about four-fifths of the birds in the author's grounds.

A species' decline along a climatic gradient is due as much to competitors and enemies being favoured as to direct harm from climate, except in Arctic, mountain or desert extremes where the struggle is with the elements.
Many checks acting at different life stages and seasons determine each species' numbers or existence, with some checks usually most potent, and different checks may act in different districts.
Dependence between beings usually lies between forms remote in nature, but the struggle is almost always most severe between individuals of the same species, which share districts, food and dangers.
A corollary of the highest importance is that the structure of every organic being is related, often in hidden ways, to that of all other beings it competes with, escapes from or preys on.

We must keep in mind that every being strives to increase geometrically and suffers destruction at some period, yet the war of nature is not incessant, death is generally prompt, and the vigorous, healthy and happy survive and multiply.
